title: Why hot things glow
interaction: Slide the temperature of an iron bar from a warm room up through a toaster element, a candle flame, a light-bulb filament and the surface of the Sun: its glow is worked out from the real law for hot bodies and turned into the colour you would see, nothing, then dull red, orange, yellow, white, blue-white. Switch to a thermal camera and see that the bar was glowing in infrared all along, even at room temperature. Line up a candle, a bulb and the Sun to read their temperatures from their colours.
takeaway: Hot things glow with a colour set by their temperature, red-hot is cooler than white-hot, and even things too cool to see are glowing in infrared.
needs: The CIE 2012 colour-matching functions already shipped by vision-color (`cone-data.ts`, CVRL) and its `blackBody` routine, which stars already reuses.
pitfall: The tap colour code is backwards for glowing things: blue-white is hotter than red. And nothing has to be 'on fire' to glow; a toaster element and a bulb filament simply get hot.
why: PhET 'Blackbody Spectrum' https://phet.colorado.edu/en/simulations/blackbody-spectrum ; KS3 physics 'Energy' (energy transfer by radiation) https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/national-curriculum-in-england-science-programmes-of-study/national-curriculum-in-england-science-programmes-of-study
overlapWith: stars: that page colours a star by its surface temperature on the Hertzsprung-Russell diagram as one detail of a life story; this one makes the colour-temperature link the whole page, with a toaster and a bulb, and adds the infrared the eye cannot see.
needsSource: Planck's law converted to screen colour with the shipped CMFs (vision-color/colour.ts `blackBody` and `cssColour`); no new data.

title: Helicopters: a spinning wing
interaction: Spin up a helicopter's rotor and lift off: the blades are wings going round, and the faster they spin or the more they tilt, the harder they throw air down and the more the helicopter is pushed up. Tilt the whole rotor disc to slide forward, backward or sideways; then switch off the tail rotor and watch the body spin the opposite way to the blades, and turn it back on to point where you like.
takeaway: A helicopter rises by throwing air down with wings that go round, moves by tilting the whole rotor, and needs its tail rotor to stop the body spinning the other way.
pitfall: The rotor does not screw into the air like a propeller into wood; it lifts like a wing. Without the tail rotor the helicopter does not simply stop turning: the engine turning the blades one way turns the body the other, and the tail rotor's push is the only thing that cancels it.
why: Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum, 'How Things Fly', https://howthingsfly.si.edu/ ('how do helicopters fly' is a perennial search question)
overlapWith: flight: that page is a fixed wing section at level 2; this page's wing goes round, and the new ideas are the tilted disc and the body spinning the other way.
needsSource: none (rotor thrust from momentum theory)

title: Hot-air balloons: a bag of lighter air
interaction: Fire the burner under a balloon and watch the air inside warm, spread out and grow lighter than the cold air around it, until the bag, basket and passengers weigh less than the air they push aside and the whole thing lifts. Let it cool and it sinks; pull the vent to drop faster; add passengers and see how much hotter the air must be. Climb high and watch the lift fade as the outside air thins.
takeaway: A hot-air balloon floats because the warm air inside is lighter than the cool air outside, and the burner is the only control a pilot has for up and down.
pitfall: Hot air does not rise because 'heat rises': the warm air is pushed up by the heavier cold air around it, the same reason a cork comes up in water. The balloon is not sealed or pressurised; it is open at the bottom, and warm air spilling out is normal.
why: England KS3 science, the particle model: changes of density with temperature, https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/national-curriculum-in-england-science-programmes-of-study ('how do hot air balloons work' is a common search question)
overlapWith: states-of-matter: that page heats particles in a box to change state; this page heats air inside a bag and asks only whether the bag is lighter than the air outside it.
needsSource: none (air density from the ideal-gas law and a standard atmosphere)

title: Ice skates: glide forward, grip sideways
interaction: Give a sled one shove on grass, on a wooden floor, on concrete and on ice and count how far it slides on each; ice is in a class of its own. Then put on skates: a blade glides along its length but bites sideways, so pushing off at an angle sends you forward, and leaning onto an edge carves a curve, while a skater who pushes straight back goes nowhere. A zoom shows the thin wet layer on the ice that makes the gliding possible.
takeaway: Skating works because ice is uncommonly slippery along the blade while the blade's edge still grips sideways, and every push is made against that sideways grip.
needs: Measured sliding-friction coefficients for ice, wood, concrete and grass from a cited physics reference (textbook values, no dataset).
pitfall: The blade does not melt the ice by pressure: the melting-point drop under a skater is a few hundredths of a degree. Ice is slippery because its surface carries a thin liquid-like layer and rubbing warms it further, which is why flat shoes slip too.
why: Robert Rosenberg, 'Why is ice slippery?', Physics Today (2005), the standard correction of the pressure-melting story, https://physicstoday.aip.org/features/why-is-ice-slippery
overlapWith: newtons-laws: that page treats friction as a slider on a cart; this page is a surface comparison and the odd sideways grip of a blade, and it corrects the pressure-melting story.
needsSource: none (friction coefficients quoted from a cited reference)

title: Keeping things warm (and cold)
interaction: Build a container for hot tea from layers in a palette (paper, metal, foam, wool, an air gap, a vacuum gap, a lid or no lid) and start the clock: a thermometer in the tea and a plot show it cooling toward the room's temperature, fast or slow depending on the walls. Swap the tea for an ice cube and the same walls keep the cold in just as well. Compare a paper cup, a mug, a vacuum flask and a sleeping bag side by side.
takeaway: A good insulator makes no heat of its own; it slows heat on its way out, or in, so the temperature curve bends more slowly.
needs: Thermal conductivity and heat capacity for a handful of materials (handbook values).
pitfall: A coat or a blanket does not make warmth and cold is not a substance that gets in; both just slow the heat flowing between the inside and the outside, which is why a vacuum flask keeps iced water cold too.
why: NGSS MS-PS3-3: design, construct and test a device that minimises or maximises thermal energy transfer (clarification: an insulated box, a Styrofoam cup) https://learninglab.si.edu/standards/MS-PS3-3/1924 ; KS3 physics 'Energy' (energy transfer from the hotter to the cooler object; use of insulators) and KS2 Year 5 'Properties and changes of materials' (conductivity, electrical and thermal) https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/national-curriculum-in-england-science-programmes-of-study/national-curriculum-in-england-science-programmes-of-study
overlapWith: greenhouse-effect: that page balances sunlight in against infrared out for a planet; this one balances a hot drink against a room through walls the reader builds, with no sunlight and no gases.
needsSource: Lumped thermal model (heat capacities joined by the conductances of each layer, Newton's cooling at the surface). Material values from a handbook table (Wikipedia's thermal conductivity list, CC BY-SA 4.0, or a textbook); a few values only.

title: Kites: how a string holds you to the wind
interaction: Fly a kite on a line and change the wind: the kite climbs to the angle where the wind's push, its weight and the pull of the string balance, and a gauge shows the tug in your hand. Move the knot where the string joins the kite to tilt it more or less into the wind, add a tail, and find the settings that make it fly steady, nose over, or refuse to lift; cut the string and it tumbles away downwind.
takeaway: A kite flies because the wind pushes on a tilted surface and the string turns that push into lift, so no wind or no string means no kite.
pitfall: The kite does not rise because the wind blows upward: the wind is level, and the tilt of the kite turns part of its push upward. Running with a kite works only because running makes wind.
why: NASA Glenn Research Center, Beginner's Guide to Aeronautics, 'Kites', https://www.grc.nasa.gov/www/k-12/airplane/kite1.html
overlapWith: flight: that page is a wing section at level 2 with streamlines, a pressure map and stall; this page is a flat kite on a string with one control, trimmed by hand, and prepares the reader for it.
needsSource: none

title: Magnets & poles
interaction: Drag two bar magnets about on a board: arrows show the pull or push between them, computed from their poles, and a compass needle and a sprinkle of iron filings line up along the field. Flip one magnet end for end and the pull turns into a push. Slide a steel paper clip toward a magnet to see it become a magnet of its own and pick up a chain of clips, then cut a magnet in half and find that each half still has two ends.
takeaway: A magnet always has two ends; like ends push apart and unlike ends pull together, and the pull fades quickly with distance.
pitfall: A magnet does not attract all metals, only iron, steel, nickel and cobalt; and cutting a magnet never separates its poles, each piece has two.
why: NGSS 3-PS2-3 (electric or magnetic interactions between objects not in contact; the clarification names paper clips and magnets) https://www2.cde.ca.gov/cacs/id/web/29018 ; KS2 Year 3 'Forces and magnets' (magnets have two poles; predict whether two magnets attract or repel) https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/national-curriculum-in-england-science-programmes-of-study/national-curriculum-in-england-science-programmes-of-study
overlapWith: electromagnetism: that page (level 2) places charges, draws field lines and induces currents with coils; this one has no electricity at all, only permanent magnets, their two poles, what they attract and how a clip becomes a temporary magnet.
needsSource: none; the model is the two-pole (Gilbert) bar magnet with inverse-square pole forces and an induced pole pair for steel.

title: Metal detectors
interaction: Sweep a coil over a beach with coins, a ring, a bottle cap and a stone buried at different depths. The coil's pulsing magnetism is drawn reaching into the sand; when it crosses metal it stirs swirling currents in the metal, and those currents make a magnetic echo the coil hears as a tone. The stone stays silent, the aluminium cap sings though no magnet would stick to it, and the deep coin only whispers; a bigger coil reaches deeper but finds the small things less well.
takeaway: A metal detector's coil makes a changing magnetism that sets up swirling currents in any nearby metal, magnetic or not, and the echo of those currents is what it hears; nearer and bigger metal, louder echo.
needsSource: none; the target is a small conducting loop coupled to the search coil, with an echo that falls off steeply with distance (roughly the sixth power for a small target).
pitfall: It is not a magnet attracting metal: it finds gold and aluminium, which no magnet picks up. The echo fades very fast with depth, so 'it found nothing' does not mean nothing is there.
why: NGSS 3-PS2-3: 'cause and effect relationships of electric or magnetic interactions between two objects not in contact with each other' (https://www.nextgenscience.org/pe/3-ps2-3-motion-and-stability-forces-and-interactions); 'Metal detector' averaged about 6,100 views a month on English Wikipedia in 2025.
overlapWith: contactless-cards in this batch: coupled coils again, but there a chip answers on purpose while here any metal echoes. electromagnetism (level 2) induces a current in a coil from a moving magnet; the eddy-current echo is the level-0 version with no field lines.

title: Microwave oven
interaction: Switch the oven on and watch the waves from the magnetron bounce off the metal walls and add up into a fixed pattern of hot spots and quiet spots about six centimetres apart. Put in a bar of chocolate with the turntable stopped and see it melt only at the spots, then start the turntable and watch the food sweep through them; thicken the food to see the waves reach only a centimetre or two in, with the middle warming later by conduction.
takeaway: The waves in the box form a fixed pattern of hot and cold spots, so the food has to move through them, and they heat only the outer layer, from which heat spreads inward.
pitfall: Microwaves do not cook from the inside out, and 2.45 GHz is not a special resonance of water; the waves penetrate a centimetre or two and the middle of a thick food heats by conduction.
why: The chocolate-bar speed-of-light experiment is a classroom standard (National Geographic Education, https://blog.education.nationalgeographic.org/2015/04/15/a-peep-into-the-speed-of-light/; school practical at https://www.preproom.org/practicals/pr.aspx?prID=1089); 'how to use a microwave' searches rose 1,472% in the UK in 2022 (https://www.insightdiy.co.uk/news/most-googled-diy-questions-in-the-uk/11094.htm).
overlapWith: waves-interference: that page shows standing waves on a string and two-source ripples; here the standing wave fills a metal box, melts chocolate at its peaks, and the turntable is the fix.
needsSource: none

title: Mirror images
interaction: Place flat mirrors on a board between an eye and a toy: the page traces light from the toy, bounces it off each mirror and follows it back to where the eye believes the toy is, as far behind the mirror as the toy is in front. Build a periscope from two mirrors to see over a wall, then set two mirrors at a corner and count the images as you close the angle. Stand a figure with a label on its front before one mirror and see which way it turns: front to back, not left to right.
takeaway: A mirror image sits behind the mirror exactly as far as the object is in front, and bouncing light along straight lines explains periscopes and kaleidoscopes.
pitfall: A mirror does not swap left and right; it swaps front and back. And a mirror half your height shows all of you, however far you stand from it.
why: KS3 physics 'Light waves' (specular reflection at a surface; use of ray model to explain imaging in mirrors, the pinhole camera) https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/national-curriculum-in-england-science-programmes-of-study/national-curriculum-in-england-science-programmes-of-study ; KS2 Year 3 'Light' (light is reflected from surfaces), same document.
overlapWith: light-optics: that page has mirrors as one item on an optical bench beside lenses and prisms; this one is only flat mirrors, the image behind the glass, periscopes and multiple reflections, with no refraction.
needsSource: none; the law of reflection and virtual-image construction over several mirrors.

title: Noise-cancelling headphones
interaction: An aeroplane rumble reaches a drawn ear as a wave; switch the cancelling on and a tiny microphone on the headphone hears it, the speaker plays the same wave upside down, and the two add to a flat line while a meter shows how much noise is left. Now slide the noise from a low rumble to a high hiss: the headphone's copy arrives a hair late, which hardly matters for slow waves and ruins the cancellation for fast ones, so the meter climbs. Add a sudden clap and watch it get through untouched.
takeaway: Noise-cancelling headphones add a mirror image of the noise so that the two shakes sum to nothing, which works for slow steady rumbles and fails for fast hisses and sudden sounds because the copy arrives a little late.
needsSource: none; the residual of a wave plus its inverted, slightly delayed copy, swept across pitch.
pitfall: The headphones do not block sound with a wall; they add sound. High hisses are quietened by the ear cups' padding, not by cancelling; keep the two apart. Cancellation is not the noise being sucked away.
why: 'Active noise control' averaged about 7,100 views a month on English Wikipedia in 2025 (https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/metrics/pageviews/per-article/en.wikipedia/all-access/user/Active_noise_control/monthly/2025010100/2025123100).
overlapWith: waves-interference (level 1): that page shows bands of cancellation in a ripple tank; this one is the device, with the delay as the one control and 'how much is left' as the meter.

title: Mixing paints vs mixing lights
interaction: Mix two paints on paper, cyan and yellow say, and the mix is green and darker than either; the page multiplies the measured reflection of each paint colour by colour and shows what is left. Mix the same two as torch beams on a white wall and the overlap is brighter and a different colour. Add the third paint and the paper goes nearly black; add the third beam and the wall goes white.
takeaway: Lights add up and get brighter, paints each take colours away and get darker, so the same two colours mixed give different results.
needs: Measured reflectance spectra of a few artists' or printer pigments (cyan, magenta, yellow, red, blue, white, black). No openly licensed set was identified this session; the candidate is weak until one is found. The CIE colour-matching functions are already shipped by vision-color.
pitfall: The page must not teach red, yellow and blue as 'the' three primary colours: printers and painters who want the widest range use cyan, magenta and yellow, and lights use red, green and blue. Black paint is not 'all colours mixed'.
why: KS3 physics 'Light waves' (colours and the different frequencies of light; differential colour effects in absorption and diffuse reflection) https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/national-curriculum-in-england-science-programmes-of-study/national-curriculum-in-england-science-programmes-of-study ; PhET 'Color Vision' listed in the PhET middle-school guide https://phet.colorado.edu/files/guides/MiddleSchool_en.pdf
overlapWith: vision-color: that page mixes red, green and blue light to match a target with the cone responses shown; this one makes paint the core, reflection spectra multiplied, and keeps the lights only as the foil that shows why paint mixes differently.
needsSource: Additive mixing of lamp spectra and subtractive mixing by multiplying reflectance spectra (single-constant Kubelka-Munk), converted with the shipped CMFs (vision-color/cone-data.ts, CVRL). Pigment spectra: no open source confirmed; weak until one is (candidates to check: a university spectral database or a pigment-reference set with a stated licence).

title: Paper planes: finding the balance point
interaction: Throw a paper plane and watch it glide, rear up and stall, or dive, depending on where its weight sits: slide a paper clip along the nose to move the balance point and throw again, and a trace of each flight builds up. Bend the tail flaps up or down, throw harder or softer, and find the settings that give the longest, smoothest glide; a marker shows the balance point and the wing's centre as they move.
takeaway: A paper plane glides when its weight sits a little ahead of its wings, and a well-trimmed plane recovers from a bad throw by nodding back to the same path.
pitfall: A plane does not fly because air over the top must 'catch up' with air below; the wing pushes air down and the air pushes back. A harder throw does not fix a plane that is out of balance; it only makes it loop or dive sooner.
why: Bartosz Ciechanowski's interactive 'Airfoil', the explainer readers reach for on lift, https://ciechanow.ski/airfoil/ (curriculum: NGSS 3-5-ETS1-3, testing and improving a design)
overlapWith: flight: that page is the wing section itself at level 2; this page never shows the pressure map and asks the reader to trim a whole plane with a paper clip.
needsSource: none (thin-plate lift, drag and pitching moment with a simple stall, stated on the page)

title: Parachutes: why you stop speeding up
interaction: Jump from a plane and watch the speed dial climb and then stick, as the air's push back grows with speed until it matches your weight; pull the cord and a canopy opens, the push leaps, you slow hard, and the dial settles at a new, gentle speed. Try a bigger and a smaller canopy, a heavier jumper, a stone and a feather, then jump on the Moon where no air pushes back at all.
takeaway: Air pushes back harder the faster you fall, until it matches your weight and the speed stops rising, and a big canopy brings that balance at a slow speed.
pitfall: A parachute does not stop you falling or push you up: you keep falling, only slowly. After the canopy opens you slow down, you do not go up; the film of a jumper 'rising' is shot by a cameraman who is still falling fast.
why: England KS2 science, Year 5 forces: air resistance, with parachutes the standard classroom investigation, https://www.stem.org.uk/resources/community/collection/12696/year-5-forces
overlapWith: newtons-laws: that page has air resistance as a slider on a projectile; this page is one falling body, the speed dial and the moment the push balances the weight.
needsSource: none

title: Pushing a swing
interaction: Give a swing one push and watch it go back and forth at a steady rhythm; lengthen or shorten the ropes, or swap the child for an adult, and see that only the length changes the rhythm. Then tap the push button whenever you like: pushes that land at the same point of each swing make it climb, pushes at the wrong moment bring it down, and a seated rider who leans back and straightens their legs at the right moments climbs with no push at all.
takeaway: A swing's rhythm is set by its length alone, not by how hard it is pushed or who sits on it, and it climbs only when each push or pump adds a little at the same point of every swing.
pitfall: Pushing harder is not what makes a swing go higher, and a heavier child does not swing slower: timing and length are what matter.
why: PhET 'Pendulum Lab' is recommended for middle school in PhET's own teaching guide (https://phet.colorado.edu/files/guides/MiddleSchool_en.pdf); KS3 physics collections teach pendulums alongside moments and pressure (https://www.stem.org.uk/node/15878).
overlapWith: oscillations-resonance: that page plots amplitude against driving frequency with sliders for mass, stiffness and damping; here there is one push button and a rope-length slider and no plot, and the thing to see is that length sets the rhythm, pushing harder does not, and only well-timed pushes add up.
needsSource: none

title: Pressure cooker
interaction: Heat water in an open pot and watch the thermometer stop at 100 °C as the steam escapes; close the lid with its weighted valve and the trapped steam presses on the water until the valve lifts and hisses, and now the water boils hotter, near 120 °C. Put a potato in and watch it cook in a third of the time; carry the open pot up a mountain to see it boil cooler and cook slower, or choose a heavier valve weight and watch the boiling point climb until the safety valve sets the limit.
takeaway: Water boils hotter when something presses on it, and it is the hotter water, not the pressure itself, that cooks the food faster.
needs: Water's boiling temperature against pressure: the IAPWS-95 saturation data from the NIST Chemistry WebBook (SRD 69), already shipped for heat-engines (`src/routes/heat-engines/steam-data.ts`); licence as recorded in docs/DATA-SOURCES.md, NIST SRD copyright, unconfirmed. The published Antoine constants for water would do instead. Cooking time as a function of temperature is a stated simplification.
pitfall: It is not the pressure that cooks the food but the higher boiling temperature, and a pot at altitude is not 'less hot' because of thin air but because its water boils at a lower temperature.
why: Nearest standard: KS2 science Year 4 States of matter, 'measure or research the temperature at which materials change state' (primary national curriculum, https://dera.ioe.ac.uk/18300/1/PRIMARY_national_curriculum.pdf); the vapour-pressure model is first-year engineering material (https://eng.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Chemical_Engineering/Foundations_of_Chemical_and_Biological_Engineering_I_(Verret_Qiao_Barghout)/03%3A_Phase_Equilibrium/3.07%3A_Estimating_Vapour_Pressure). No page-specific signal was found before the search budget ran out.
overlapWith: states-of-matter: that page shows boiling as particles escaping a liquid in a molecular-dynamics box; this page is the boiling temperature as a dial set by pressure, with cooking time as the count.
needsSource: NIST Chemistry WebBook SRD 69 saturation data, already used by heat-engines (free access; NIST SRD copyright, recorded as unconfirmed in docs/DATA-SOURCES.md), or published Antoine constants for water

title: Roller coasters: where the heavy and floaty moments come from
interaction: Draw a track with hills, dips and a loop, let a chain haul the car to the top of the first hill, and release it: it coasts, climbs no hill taller than the first, and comes round slower each lap as rubbing steals a little. A gauge on the rider's seat shows how heavy they feel, squashed into the seat at the bottom of a dip and over the top of the loop, floating over a hump; shape the loop as a circle or a teardrop and find where the car falls off.
takeaway: After the first hill a coaster has no engine and only spends the height it was given, and the squashed and floating feelings come from the track bending the car's path.
pitfall: The car is not powered round the track and does not speed up on its own; it only trades height for speed. At the top of the loop you are held in not by a force flinging you outward but by the car going too fast to fall away from the track.
why: PhET 'Energy Skate Park: Basics', in PhET's elementary-school simulation guide, https://phet.colorado.edu/en/simulations/energy-skate-park-basics
overlapWith: newtons-laws: that page already has an editable track with energy bars; this page keeps the track but drops the bars for the rider's felt weight, the loop and the first-hill rule, as one toy.
needsSource: none

title: Sailing against the wind
interaction: Turn a sailboat's heading on a pond with the wind blowing from the top and watch where it goes: downwind it is pushed along; across the wind the sail becomes a wing and the keel stops the boat sliding sideways, so it squirts forward like a pip squeezed between finger and thumb; point straight into the wind and the sail flaps and the boat stops. Zigzag to a buoy upwind and count the tacks; take away the keel and the boat slides sideways instead.
takeaway: A sailboat cannot point straight into the wind, but with the sail acting as a wing and the keel refusing to slide sideways it can zigzag its way upwind.
pitfall: Upwind the sail is not pushed from behind; it is pulled like a wing, and without the keel that pull slides the boat sideways. There is a wedge of headings into the wind where no sail works, and the only way through it is to zigzag.
why: UNSW School of Physics, 'The physics of sailing', https://www.phys.unsw.edu.au/~jw/sailing.html ('how do sailboats sail upwind' is a perennial explainer question)
overlapWith: flight: that page explains a wing's lift at level 2; this page uses two wings, one in air and one in water, and the only control is where the boat points.
needsSource: none

title: Seatbelts & airbags
interaction: Drive a car with a dummy into a wall at a chosen speed and watch the car crumple to a stop in a short distance while the dummy keeps going at the old speed until something stops it: the dashboard, a belt, or a belt and an airbag. A gauge shows how hard each one pushes on the dummy and over what distance; then pull the belt from its reel slowly and fast to see the little pendulum or spinning weight lock the ratchet.
takeaway: Nothing throws you forward in a crash; you simply keep going while the car stops, and the longer the distance over which something stops you, the gentler the push.
pitfall: You are not 'thrown forward' by the crash, and the belt does not lock because you pull hard: it locks on a sudden jerk or a sharp slowing of the car, however light the pull.
why: 'How a seat belt works' is set reading in driver-education curricula (Montana OPI module 2.1, https://opifiles.mt.gov/portals/182/Page%20Files/Driver%20Education/Curriculum/Module%202%20all%20files/2.1-How-Seat-Belts-Work.pdf) and a standing explainer topic (https://engineerfix.com/how-a-seat-belt-works-the-mechanics-explained/).
overlapWith: newtons-laws: that page collides carts of different mass; here the reader is the cart, and the control is the distance over which they are stopped.
needsSource: none

title: Shadows & pinholes
interaction: Drag a lamp, a toy and a wall about a room: straight rays from the lamp are blocked by the toy, and the shadow on the wall grows as the lamp comes closer and shrinks as the wall comes closer. Swap the small bulb for a wide lampshade and the shadow's edge goes soft; switch on a second lamp and a second shadow appears. Poke a pinhole in a shoebox and the picture of the lamp forms upside down on its back wall.
takeaway: Light travels in straight lines, so a shadow is simply where the lines are blocked, and its size follows the lines back to the lamp.
pitfall: A shadow is not something a lamp throws onto a wall; it is where no light arrives. And the Moon's phases are not Earth's shadow (the page should point to sun-earth-moon for eclipses, which are).
why: Bartosz Ciechanowski, 'Lights and Shadows' https://ciechanow.ski/lights-and-shadows/ ; KS2 Year 3 'Light' (find patterns in the way the size of shadows change) and Year 6 'Light' (light appears to travel in straight lines; shadows have the shape of the objects that cast them) https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/national-curriculum-in-england-science-programmes-of-study/national-curriculum-in-england-science-programmes-of-study
overlapWith: light-optics: that page bends rays through lenses and prisms on an optical bench; this one never bends a ray, only blocks it, and is about shadow size, soft edges and the pinhole picture.
needsSource: none; ray projection from a point or extended source past polygons onto a wall (umbra and penumbra).

title: What a smoke alarm senses
interaction: Open a smoke alarm into two little chambers: in the first, a speck of a safe radioactive metal knocks bits of air into charged pieces that drift across a gap and make a tiny steady trickle of current, and in the second a lamp shines across a dark box past a sensor that sees nothing. Blow smoke in: in the first chamber the smoke particles grab the charged bits and the trickle drops, in the second the smoke scatters light onto the sensor, and either sounds the alarm. Slide from the thin smoke of a smouldering sofa to the smoke of a flaming pan and see which chamber reacts first.
takeaway: A smoke alarm does not smell smoke: it either notices that smoke has caught the charged air crossing a gap, or sees light bounced off smoke in a dark box, and the two kinds notice different fires first.
needsSource: none beyond published figures: an americium-241 source of about 37 kBq, and the ionisation-first for flaming fires, photoelectric-first for smouldering fires result of NIST's comparison, as quoted on Wikipedia's Smoke detector page (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smoke_detector).
pitfall: The radioactive speck is tiny and the alarm is safe to live with; say so plainly. Neither kind detects heat or gas (carbon monoxide alarms are a different device). The chirp at night is a low battery, not smoke.

title: Headphones, speakers and microphones
interaction: Drag a slider back and forth to push current through a coil glued to a paper cone sitting in a magnet: the cone follows your hand in and out, and the air in front of it is shown as dots bunching and spreading as the push travels away. Let the page wiggle the current for you: faster wiggles give a higher note, bigger wiggles a louder one, and the dots show the same. Then unplug the battery, tap the cone, and watch a small current appear in the coil: the speaker has become a microphone.
takeaway: A speaker is a magnet shoving a cone in and out exactly as fast as the sound wiggles, air passes the shove along, and a microphone is the same thing run backwards.
needsSource: none; the force on a current-carrying coil in the magnet's field, a mass-and-spring cone, and a one-dimensional pressure wave in front of it.
pitfall: The cone does not blow air across the room: each bit of air only shakes in place and passes the shake on. Bigger is not louder by itself; loudness is how hard the cone moves. The earpiece in headphones is the same device shrunk, not a different mechanism.
why: England KS3 physics: 'sound produced by vibrations of objects, in loudspeakers, detected by their effects on microphone diaphragm and the ear drum' (https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/national-curriculum-in-england-science-programmes-of-study/national-curriculum-in-england-science-programmes-of-study).
overlapWith: motors-generators (level 2) is the same reversibility with a rotating coil and a commutator; waves-interference (level 1) makes sound waves in a ripple tank. This page is one coil on a cone, with the reader's hand as the signal; the physics lens's sound-is-a-shake candidate is the air alone, and this is the device.

title: Why a spinning top stays up
interaction: Flick a top with a chosen spin and watch it stand; tip it with a nudge and instead of falling over it leans and slowly wobbles round in a circle. As friction slows the spin the wobble widens and quickens, until the top finally topples. Try a gyroscope held by one end and a bicycle wheel held by its axle, run by the same equations.
takeaway: A spinning thing resists being tipped: a push on it turns into a slow sideways wobble, and it falls over only once the spin runs down.
pitfall: Spinning does not make the top lighter or cancel gravity; gravity pulls on it the whole time, and the top answers by wobbling round instead of falling.
why: Signal not verified this session (web-search budget was exhausted before the gyroscope searches ran); expected signals: Veritasium's gyroscopic-precession videos and the Wikipedia 'Gyroscope' and 'Top' articles. Ciechanowski's 'Bicycle' explainer is verified in his archive listing https://ciechanow.ski/bicycle/ (content not checked this session).
overlapWith: sun-earth-moon: that page keeps Earth's tilted axis pointing the same way as it orbits, which is this effect at planet scale, while this one spins a toy on a table and shows the wobble and the fall; among proposed pages, balance-and-tipping tips things that are not spinning.
needsSource: none; the heavy symmetric top (Euler's equations with the torque of gravity and a friction torque), integrated in real time.

title: Springs & spring scales
interaction: Hang weights on a spring one at a time and watch it stretch the same extra amount for each one, so a ruler beside it becomes a scale; swap in a stiffer spring, or put two springs side by side or end to end, and compare how far they stretch for the same weights. Load it past its limit and see it stay stretched when the weights come off; then press a bathroom scale, a mattress and a pogo stick and watch the same rule at work.
takeaway: A spring stretches by the same extra amount for each extra weight, which is what makes it a scale, until it is pulled past the point where it stops coming back.
pitfall: A spring does not push back with the same force however far it is stretched, and one stretched past its limit is not broken but bent: it still works, from a new rest length.
why: PhET 'Hooke's Law' is the standard primary and middle-school simulation of springs (https://www.compadre.org/Precollege/items/similar.cfm?ID=14156); KS2 Year 5 forces collections add springs to levers, pulleys and gears (https://stem.org.uk/node/12033).
overlapWith: oscillations-resonance: that page sets a spring bouncing and plots its response; this page never lets it move: it is the stretch per weight that makes a scale, and the limit beyond which it stays bent.
needsSource: none

title: Submarines: sinking and rising on purpose
interaction: Flood a submarine's tanks with sea water and it grows heavier than the water it pushes aside and sinks; blow the water out with compressed air and it rises; let in just enough and it hovers, neither rising nor sinking. Tilt the fins and drive forward to glide up or down; a pair of scales shows the submarine's weight against the weight of water it displaces at every moment. Hover, then add a small extra load and watch what happens.
takeaway: A submarine goes down and up by changing its own weight with water taken in or pushed out, until it weighs just as much as the water it displaces.
pitfall: A submarine does not sink because it is made of steel: full of air it floats like a ship, and it only sinks when water replaces the air. Hovering is a knife edge: a little too heavy and it keeps sinking, which is why submarines trim constantly.
why: PhET 'Buoyancy: Basics', in PhET's middle-school simulation list, https://phet.colorado.edu/en/simulations/buoyancy-basics ('how do submarines sink and float' is a common search question)
overlapWith: newtons-laws: that page balances forces on carts; here the two forces are the submarine's weight and the water's upward push, and the reader changes one of them. Floating itself is not in the catalogue; this is the one vehicle that floats, sinks and hovers by choice.
